name: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies
info: The Bourbon kingdom of Naples and Sicily, the largest state in Italy before unification, which built the peninsula's first railway and fell to Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand in 1860.

facts.founder: Ferdinand I (Ferdinand IV of Naples), who merged the Kingdom of Naples and the Kingdom of Sicily in 1816
facts.predecessor: The Kingdom of Naples (under Joseph Bonaparte and Joachim Murat 1806–1815) and the Kingdom of Sicily, both Bourbon realms since 1734
facts.successor: The Kingdom of Sardinia, which became the Kingdom of Italy in 1861

t: Ferdinand I created the kingdom in 1816 by annulling the Sicilian constitution of 1812 and merging the Kingdom of Naples and the Kingdom of Sicily into one state ruled from Naples.
The Naples–Portici line of 1839 was the first railway on the Italian peninsula, yet by 1859 the kingdom had only 99 kilometres of track against Piedmont's 850.
Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand took Sicily in 1860 and won the Battle of the Volturno with half its army local volunteers; Francis II surrendered at Gaeta in February 1861.
dyk: Sicily's mines near Catania and Agrigento supplied most of the world's sulphur; when Ferdinand II granted a French company the monopoly in 1840, breaking an 1816 trade agreement with Britain, the Sulphur Crisis followed and was settled only by French mediation.
ev: Ferdinand IV annuls the Sicilian constitution of 1812, merges Naples and Sicily into the Regno delle Due Sicilie and takes the title Ferdinand I.
A Carbonari revolution forces Ferdinand to grant the Spanish constitution of 1812 on 13 July; a rising in Palermo the same month is quickly suppressed.
Ferdinand cancels the constitution on 23 February before 50,000 Austrian troops, who enter Naples on 24 March after smashing General Guglielmo Pepe's resistance.
The railway from Naples to Portici opens, the first on the Italian peninsula, and the main streets of Naples are lit by gas.
Rebellion in Palermo on 12 January demands the 1812 constitution; Ferdinand II grants a liberal ministry, declares war on Austria on 7 April, then turns the Swiss Guard on Naples on 15 May.
Britain and France break off diplomatic relations after the kingdom refuses to release its political prisoners.
Giuseppe Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand lands in Sicily, crosses to the mainland and wins the Battle of the Volturno; at Teano he hands the kingdom to Victor Emmanuel.
Francis II surrenders and abdicates at Gaeta in February; the Two Sicilies are annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia, proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy.

sections.foundation:
The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies was made in 1816, when the Bourbon Ferdinand IV of Naples, restored to his mainland throne by the Treaty of Casalanza and given back the island of Sicily, annulled the Sicilian constitution of 1812 that had virtually disempowered him there and merged his two realms into one state, the Regno delle Due Sicilie, taking the title Ferdinand I. The name reached back to the War of the Sicilian Vespers (1282–1302), after which the Angevin rulers of Naples and the Aragonese rulers of the island each called their realm the Kingdom of Sicily, so the two were known together as Utraque Sicilia, “both Sicilies”.

The Bourbons had ruled in Naples since Infante Charles defeated the Austrians at Bitonto in 1734, the first king in over 230 years to live and rule there in person; when he became King of Spain in 1759 he left the crown to his younger son Ferdinand IV, since treaties forbade uniting Spain with Naples-Sicily. Driven out in the Napoleonic years, Ferdinand kept some of the reforms of Kings Joseph and Joachim Murat to the civil, penal and commercial codes and extended them to Sicily, but inherited brigandage and the forcible occupation of lands. The new kingdom was the largest sovereign state in Italy by population and area, covering Sicily and virtually all the peninsula south of the Papal States, with Naples, Italy's biggest city, as its capital.
sections.socioeconomy:
The population rose from about five to seven million in the nineteenth century, roughly 36 per cent of Italy's around 1850, though figures before a statistical department was founded after 1848 rest on estimates. Naples had over 400,000 inhabitants, the third largest city in Europe; Palermo was Italy's third. The economy was agricultural and protectionist. Land lay in the hands of a few noble families, and the villages housed a large rural proletariat dependent on landlords for work. Wheat, wine, olive oil and cotton were the chief products: 67 million litres of oil in 1844, mostly from Apulia and Calabria, and 191 million litres of wine.

Industry was scattered but real. The shipyard of Castellammare di Stabia employed 1,800 workers; Pietrarsa, the largest plant on the peninsula, made tools, cannon, rails and locomotives; the Mongiana ironworks in Calabria, founded in 1770, employed 1,600 in 1860 and rolled the rails of the first Italian railways. Swiss entrepreneurs ran a textile hub around Salerno. Sicilian sulphur met most of the world's demand. With every major city a port, the kingdom owned the largest merchant fleet in the Mediterranean, yet poor interior roads hampered internal trade, and by 1859 it had only 99 kilometres of railway against Piedmont's 850. Schooling was not compulsory: 2,010 primary schools served nine million people in 1859, and literacy stood at 14.4 per cent in 1861.
sections.military:
The Army of the Two Sicilies descended from the force the Bourbons settled in southern Italy after the War of the Polish Succession, and at its peak the kingdom kept 100,000 soldiers and a large bureaucracy. The Real Marina was the most important of the pre-unification Italian navies. The army's record was one of internal repression. It put down the Calabrian revolution of 1847, the Sicilian independence revolution of 1848 and, with hired Swiss Guards, the Neapolitan revolution of May 1848, retaking the mainland by July, Messina by September and Palermo on 15 May 1849.

Against the Carbonari rising of 1820–1821 it had been less sure: resistance by regular forces under General Guglielmo Pepe and irregular Carbonari was smashed by the 50,000 Austrian troops who entered Naples on 24 March 1821, and the Congress of Vienna had given Austria the right to station troops in the kingdom, which it did until 1827. The war declared on Austria on 7 April 1848, under the pressure of public sentiment, was fought on paper only. When Giuseppe Garibaldi landed in Sicily in 1860 at the head of the Expedition of the Thousand, with the connivance of Cavour, many rallied to him; he crossed to the mainland and won the Battle of the Volturno with half his army local volunteers, and the Bourbon army collapsed. King Francis II withdrew to the fortified port of Gaeta and surrendered after the Siege of Gaeta in February 1861.
sections.governance:
The Two Sicilies was an absolute monarchy under the House of Bourbon-Two Sicilies, a cadet branch of the Bourbons, ruled by Ferdinand I (1816–1825), Francis I (1825–1830), Ferdinand II (1830–1859) and Francis II (1859–1861). The Congress of Vienna had granted Austria the right to station troops, and Austria, Russia and Prussia insisted that no written constitution be given. Administratively Naples and Sicily remained separate units, the peninsula in fifteen departments and Sicily in seven; Sicily kept a secondary and semi-colonial status beneath the court at Naples.

Open political activity was suppressed, so liberals organised in secret societies such as the Carbonari, outlawed in 1816. Their rising of 1820 forced Ferdinand I to grant the Spanish constitution of 1812 on 13 July, which he cancelled on 23 February 1821 before Austrian bayonets; repression then deepened. Ferdinand II began with a political amnesty and tax cuts, but after the revolution of 1848, when he appointed a liberal prime minister and broke with Austria only to turn the Swiss Guard on Naples on 15 May, he governed cautiously and authoritatively to forestall another rising. More than half the deputies elected in 1848 were arrested or fled, and the treatment of political prisoners and “suspicious elements” violated the constitution's guarantees. Clerics inspected the schools and held a veto over the appointment of teachers, who were mostly clergy.
sections.impact:
The Two Sicilies left its deepest mark in music and in a record of Italian firsts. The Real Teatro di San Carlo, opened on 4 November 1737 as the biggest opera house in the world, was rebuilt within ten months of the fire of 13 February 1816 by Antonio Niccolini as a horseshoe of 1,444 seats. Gioachino Rossini was house composer and artistic director of the royal opera houses from 1815 to 1822 and wrote ten operas there; Domenico Barbaja's offer brought Gaetano Donizetti to Naples until 1844, where 51 of his operas were presented, and Vincenzo Bellini's first professionally staged opera opened at the San Carlo on 30 May 1826.

The kingdom built the first railway on the Italian peninsula, from Naples to Portici in 1839, the first iron suspension bridge in Italy, the Real Ferdinando Bridge, and the first volcano observatory in the world, the Osservatorio Vesuviano, in 1841. Its sulphur fed Britain's industrialisation after the repeal of the salt tariffs in 1824, and Ferdinand II's grant of a monopoly to a French company in 1840 brought the Sulphur Crisis with Britain. Gladstone's letters from Naples in 1850, calling the government “the negation of God erected to a system of government”, helped isolate the kingdom before its conquest, and the title of King of the Two Sicilies is still claimed by the head of the House of Bourbon-Two Sicilies.
sections.decline:
The kingdom's political movements had been Neapolitan or Sicilian rather than Italian: Sicily in 1848–1849 sought independence from Naples, not a united Italy, and public feeling for unification was low, so the Two Sicilies did not figure in Cavour's early plans. What undid it was isolation abroad and repression at home. Ferdinand II kept the political prisoners whose release Britain and France demanded in 1856, and both powers broke off relations. Only when Austria was defeated in 1859 and the north, Venetia apart, was united in 1860 did Garibaldi launch the Expedition of the Thousand against Sicily with Cavour's connivance. Many rallied to him, and after Sicily he won the Battle of the Volturno on the mainland.

Francis II withdrew to the fortified port of Gaeta, where he surrendered and abdicated in February 1861 after the Siege of Gaeta. At the encounter of Teano Garibaldi met King Victor Emmanuel and handed him the conquered kingdom; the people voted in a plebiscite to join the Kingdom of Sardinia, and the annexation completed the first phase of Italian unification, the Kingdom of Italy being proclaimed in 1861. The south entered the new state with its land concentrated in few hands, cities with little industry to absorb a countryside growing faster than Naples itself, 99 kilometres of railway and a literacy rate of 14.4 per cent. The Bourbon claim to the throne survives in the House of Bourbon-Two Sicilies.

summary: The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies united Naples and Sicily under the Bourbons from 1816, the largest state in pre-unification Italy, home to the San Carlo opera, Italy's first railway and most of the world's sulphur; absolutist and repressive, it crushed the revolutions of 1820 and 1848 but fell to Garibaldi's Thousand in 1860 and was annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1861.
references: Louis Mendola, The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies 1734–1861 (Trinacria Editions, 2019)
Lucy Riall, Sicily and the Unification of Italy: Liberal Policy and Local Power, 1859–1866 (Clarendon Press, 1998)
M. I. Finley, Denis Mack Smith and Christopher Duggan, A History of Sicily (Chatto & Windus, 1986)
Girolamo Imbruglia (ed.), Naples in the Eighteenth Century: The Birth and Death of a Nation State (Cambridge University Press, 2000)

pointDescs.1816: Ferdinand IV annuls the Sicilian constitution of 1812 and merges Naples and Sicily into the Regno delle Due Sicilie as Ferdinand I; it is the largest state in Italy by population and area.
pointDescs.1820: A Carbonari revolution forces Ferdinand I to grant the Spanish constitution of 1812 on 13 July; a rising in Palermo is suppressed, and the Holy Alliance at Troppau decides to intervene.
pointDescs.1821: Ferdinand cancels the constitution on 23 February; 50,000 Austrian troops smash General Pepe's resistance and enter Naples on 24 March. Repression intensifies.
pointDescs.1828: A coup to force a constitution is suppressed by Neapolitan troops alone, the Austrian army having left the year before.
pointDescs.1830: Ferdinand II succeeds Francis I, declares a political amnesty and cuts taxes to stimulate the economy.
pointDescs.1839: The Naples–Portici railway, the first on the Italian peninsula, opens and the main streets of Naples are gas-lit; the kingdom's merchant fleet is the largest in the Mediterranean.
pointDescs.1840: Ferdinand II grants a French company a monopoly on Sicilian sulphur, breaking the 1816 agreement with Britain; the Sulphur Crisis is settled by French mediation.
pointDescs.1848: Palermo rises on 12 January; Ferdinand II appoints a liberal ministry and declares war on Austria on 7 April, then has the Swiss Guard suppress the revolution in Naples on 15 May.
pointDescs.1849: Palermo, the revolutionaries' last stronghold, falls on 15 May; the kingdom has crushed the revolution and the Sicilian secession with its own forces.
pointDescs.1856: Britain and France demand the release of political prisoners and, refused, break off diplomatic relations; Gladstone's letters of 1850 have already isolated the kingdom.
pointDescs.1859: Francis II succeeds Ferdinand II; Austria is defeated in the north and the kingdom's isolation deepens, with 99 kilometres of railway against Piedmont's 850.
pointDescs.1860: Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand takes Sicily and wins the Battle of the Volturno; Francis II withdraws to Gaeta and Garibaldi hands the kingdom to Victor Emmanuel at Teano.
pointDescs.1861: Francis II surrenders and abdicates at Gaeta in February; the Two Sicilies are annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia, which becomes the Kingdom of Italy.

notes: The kings' regnal dates are taken from the article (Francis I 1825–1830; Francis II 'since 1859'); the article gives Ferdinand II's reign only by those bounds.
The Battle of the Volturno and the encounter of Teano are undated in the article beyond 1860; the Siege of Gaeta ends in February 1861.
The article says the Austrian army left 'the previous year' before the 1828 coup, i.e. 1827.
The article mentions a 1836 cholera epidemic (65,000 dead in Sicily) and the Calabrian insurrection of September 1847, left out of the sections for space.
The 'Southern Question' appears in the article only in a reference title, so the decline section describes the inherited inequalities without naming it.
